in 2023, 58,337 households in Essex, equating to 9% of all households - were living in fuel poverty, meaning they could not afford to heat their homes adequately. This represents a decrease of 0.3 percentage points (1,381 households) compared to 2022. The difference between the level of fuel poverty reported to CDP last year (21.5% based on 2021 projections) and the level reported this year reflects a change in the definition of fuel poverty used.by the UK government. After 2021, the government replaced the 10% affordability threshold (which classified households as fuel poor if they needed to spend more than 10% of their income on energy ) and now uses the Low-Income Low Energy Efficiency (LILEE) indicator. Under this metric, a household is considered fuel poor if:

1.	The home has a Fuel Poverty Energy Efficiency Rating (FPEER) of band D or below, and 
2.	Residual income after housing and modelled energy costs is below the official poverty line.

This is the metric now used by ECC.

The National Energy and Climate Plan lacks definitions, key indicators and targets to combat energy poverty. 

In Denmark, energy poverty is mainly addressed through social policies. Households in a difficult economic situation may apply for financial assistance from municipalities as part of the Danish social security system. Targeted financial support is available for low-income pensioners to receive a reimbursement for heating-related expenses. Multiple programmes exist to improve the energy efficiency of housing. 

The new EU energy efficiency directive will require member countries to have a definition and adress the issue, therefore Copenhagen is attempting to work on this issue in a coordinated way with the national government if possible. 

Copenhagen is covered almost 100% by district heating, and according to the Danish Heat Supply law, utilities are required to choose the cheapest energy source whenever they make an investment. District heating is therefore the cheapest heat supply option. The city is working to keep a district heating coverage close to 100% through the climate plan. See for example: https://www.kk.dk/sites/default/files/agenda/9d967322-92f7-4e9c-892e-3ed6a62a9eee/bd8e07b4-01d6-4233-a9d1-f92bdd5185a3-bilag-2.pdf; https://www.kk.dk/sites/default/files/agenda/80713a4c-1ae1-42f0-95aa-e67228ade379/587bf2a7-8734-4260-a59a-65097c1e6609-bilag-2.pdf; 
https://www.kk.dk/dagsordener-og-referater/Teknik-%20og%20Milj%C3%B8udvalget/m%C3%B8de-30092024/referat/punkt-5.

A household is regarded as being in fuel poverty if they are unable to keep their home warm at a reasonable cost. In Wales, this is measured as any household that would have to spend more than 10% of their income on maintaining a satisfactory heating regime. Any household having to spend more than 20% is defined as being in severe fuel poverty. A household needing to spend between 8 and 10% is classed as being at risk of fuel poverty (i.e. they are susceptible to relatively small changes in income or energy costs). 

Data estimate obtained from: https://www.gov.wales/fuel-poverty-interactive-dashboard

The Act defines fuel poverty for a household as being where the fuel costs necessary for the home to meet a reasonable condition of heat are more than 10% of the households adjusted net income.

Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Scottish House Condition Survey have not been able to collate information as expected; therefore we won't have access to a more recent dataset until 2026 when fuel poverty rates at a local authority level are next expected to be be released.

In Johannesburg, around 19.4% of households rely on indirect electricity sources such as a neighbour or landlord rather than having their own direct mains connection

This is nearly double the average for South African metros (10.7%) and highlights a persistent form of energy poverty in the city.
Several drivers contribute to this situation:
Rapid urbanisation and in-migration into Johannesburg have led to rising household numbers that often outpace formal electrification programmes.
Informal settlements and backyard dwellings are widespread, where residents frequently depend on shared or informal connections due to the absence of formal grid infrastructure.
Affordability constraints force many low-income households to forgo direct accounts with utilities, relying instead on landlords or neighbours to mediate electricity access.
Service delivery backlogs and housing informality also play a role, with electrification lagging behind demand in high-density urban areas.
Together, these factors mean that while Johannesburg's overall electrification rate is high, one in five households remains energy poor, dependent on precarious and often unsafe energy arrangements.

- 17,505 (1.51%) households with energy poverty live in apartments
- 28,765 (2.48%) households with energy poverty live in Core Housing Need
- 7,125 (0.61%) households with energy poverty live in Major Repair Need
- 68,255 (5.88%) households with energy poverty live in Older Housing
- 32,150 (2.77%) households with energy poverty live in households with no English/French (official languages) spoken at home
- 9,285 (0.80%) households with energy poverty have Newcomers living in them
- 21,005 (1.81%) households with energy poverty have Renters living in them
- 39,910 (3.44%) households with energy poverty have Seniors living in them
- 10,305 (0.89%) households with energy poverty have Single-parents living in them

Source: Efficiency Canada (2025). Energy Poverty in Canada. Available at: https://www.efficiencycanada.org/energy-poverty-in-canada/

column17: INSEE estimates that approximately 70,000 people are in a situation of fuel poverty in Paris, meaning that they are unable to meet their basic energy needs in their homes (INSEE 2018). This problem combines three factors: low income, poor thermal quality of housing and the cost of final energy for the inhabitant. Nevertheless, the INSEE definition of fuel poverty does not take into account other forms of fuel poverty related to insufficient or inadequate heating, defective or even health-endangering ventilation, or very degraded summer comfort in housing during hot weather.The City of Paris is already working effectively to help disadvantaged households, in particular through the numerous aids that exist to support households in a situation of energy insecurity (the Fonds de Solidarité Logement, Paris Énergie Familles or the exceptional allowance of the City of Paris). Energy poverty is an increasingly important issue for Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (ABB), particularly in the context of rising global energy prices, limited energy efficiency in the existing building stock, and the socio-economic vulnerabilities of certain household groups. Although Turkey has achieved almost universal household access to modern energy services such as electricity and natural gas (>99% connection rates in urban areas), the affordability dimension remains a major challenge. Energy poverty in Ankara is therefore not a matter of access but of financial ability to maintain secure, sustainable, and affordable energy services.

In line with international definitions, ABB uses the “10% income threshold” to identify energy poverty, meaning households spending 10% or more of their disposable income on energy services (heating, cooling, lighting, cooking, and appliances). This threshold is widely used in both the European Union (EU) and national academic research. Based on available statistics from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TurkStat/TÜİK) Household Budget Surveys, as well as independent studies carried out under the European Energy Poverty Observatory (EPOV) and national energy economics research, approximately 15% of households in Ankara can be considered energy poor according to this indicator. While this share is lower than rural and less developed regions in Turkey, it still represents a significant number of households across the capital city.

The main drivers of energy poverty in Ankara are:

Low household income: Vulnerable groups, including unemployed individuals, retirees, and informal sector workers, are most affected.

High energy costs: Natural gas and electricity tariffs have increased significantly since 2018, creating affordability pressures.

Inefficient building stock: Many residential buildings constructed before 2000 lack adequate insulation, efficient heating systems, or renewable integration.

Limited awareness and behavioral factors: Households may not fully utilize available subsidies, energy-saving devices, or renewable energy programs.

ABB has integrated the energy poverty dimension into its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP, also referred to as YIDEP - Ankara's Local Climate Action Plan). Actions in the plan directly or indirectly reduce household exposure to energy poverty by lowering energy bills, improving efficiency, or supporting vulnerable groups. Key initiatives include:

Building energy efficiency programs: Promoting retrofits, insulation, and replacement of inefficient boilers with modern, cleaner systems.

Support for renewable energy deployment: Expanding solar PV for public buildings, rural cooperatives, and agricultural irrigation, which helps reduce dependency on expensive fossil fuels.

Public transport and mobility improvements: Expanding bus, metro, and bicycle infrastructure, reducing household transport-related energy costs.

Awareness campaigns: Water and energy-saving initiatives by Ankara Water and Sewerage Administration (ASKI) and other municipal subsidiaries.

Social support programs: Targeted subsidies for low-income groups, especially in heating and electricity, in coordination with national government programs.

The municipality also collaborates with Middle East Technical University (METU), civil society organizations, and professional chambers to better assess the scale of energy poverty, monitor indicators, and design cost-effective interventions. ABB is aligning its monitoring approach with the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM) Common Reporting Framework (CRF) to ensure international comparability and transparency.

While no official nationwide definition of energy poverty currently exists in Turkey, ABB acknowledges the urgency of addressing this issue as part of climate action, sustainable development, and social equity. In practice, energy poverty in Ankara is monitored through household expenditure surveys and qualitative assessments conducted under SECAP/YIDEP. The municipality recognizes that energy poverty is not only an economic and social challenge but also an environmental one: households with limited financial capacity may rely on inefficient heating devices or low-quality fuels, leading to higher emissions and worsening air quality.

Going forward, ABB plans to:

Conduct regular local surveys to complement national data and obtain more granular understanding of household energy expenditures.

Explore new indicators beyond the 10% threshold, such as the “Low Income High Costs” (LIHC) approach used in the UK or multidimensional energy poverty indicators (MEPI), to better capture hidden vulnerabilities.

Strengthen cooperation with development agencies and national ministries to channel funding towards building retrofits and clean energy access programs.

The City of Cape Town does not currently formally measure energy poverty. However, there have been efforts made to understand the extent of energy poverty in Cape Town. Although Cape Town has one of the highest electrification rates in the country, at 96.7% in 2022, an estimated 70 000 households are not connected to grid electricity. Of these, an estimated 13 335 (2022/2023) households are located in informal settlements that cannot be provided electricity from the grid due to their location on land unsuited to development (located on wetlands, former landfills, etc.). 
At present, these residents are left more vulnerable to energy poverty relative to those that have access to grid electricity because they do not have access to an energy poverty relief subsidy and are subject to high local prices for heating fuels. Around 250,000 households rent space informally in so-called 'backyards' or in multi-unit structures. The majority that are connected access electricity through the main connection of a landlord. Due to the absence of a formal connection, the occupants are vulnerable to exploitation from landlords. The landlords may opt to cut off electricity supply whenever they want in the absence of rent payments or charge exorbitant rates for electricity, without adhering to regulated prices. Additionally, occupants of these units do not have access to the subsidized electricity tariff and free basic electricity that the City provides to low-income households.

The expenditure-based approach that defines energy poverty by the share of total household income used to purchase energy is most widely used in South Africa. Households spending more than 10% of their income on energy are classified as energy poor (using this measure about 40% of the population is energy poor). However, using the expenditure-based approach to understand energy poverty in Cape Town has proven to be sub-optimal in understanding its extent. Several studies with varying results indicate a wide variation of household energy expenditure across low-income households.

column17:
Energy poverty in the City of Ljubljana is regulated in accordance with Slovenian legislation. Energy poverty is defined as a social issue where households are unable to provide an adequate energy supply for basic needs, such as heating, cooling, lighting, and the use of household appliances, due to low income, high energy costs, and poor energy efficiency of residential units. Energy poverty is primarily addressed in the Energy Act (EZ-1) and the National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP).

The Energy Act (EZ-1) stipulates that the state must implement measures to reduce energy poverty, which includes promoting energy efficiency, providing financial assistance to energy-poor households, and supporting energy renovation of residential buildings. It also emphasizes the right of access to basic energy services, particularly for vulnerable groups, such as the elderly, low-income households, and persons with disabilities.

The NECP identifies energy poverty as one of the key challenges in ensuring a fair transition to a low-carbon society. The NECP sets out goals and measures to reduce energy poverty, including improving energy efficiency in households, providing financial support for the energy renovation of buildings, and promoting the use of renewable energy sources.

In addition, the Resolution on the National Program for Social Protection also highlights the need to reduce energy poverty as part of broader social justice and vulnerable group protection policies. Measures such as subsidizing energy costs and renovating housing are key instruments for reducing energy poverty in Slovenia.

Methodology: According to the Decree on the Criteria for Defining and Assessing the Number of Energy-Poor Households (Official Gazette of the Republic of Slovenia, No. 132/2022 of October 14, 2022), households are defined as energy-poor if their income in the year prior to the Life Conditions Survey (EU-SILC) was below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold and they met at least one of the following three conditions: they were financially unable to maintain a properly heated home; they were late with payments for housing costs (such as utilities, water, electricity, heating, etc., including energy services) due to financial difficulties in the last 12 months before the survey; or they lived in housing with a leaking roof, damp walls/floors/foundations, or rotting window frames/floors (inadequate living conditions).

The data source is the EU-harmonised Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC) survey. The 2024 data were obtained from the 2024 EU-SILC questionnaire (year of data collection) and from registers and administrative sources, which mostly refer to 2023 (the income reference year). The at-risk-of-poverty threshold for 2024 is calculated on the basis of (net) disposable household incomes received in 2023.

Data source: https://www.stat.si/StatWeb/news/Index/13487

For single family households living in houses the enery poverty level in the project was estimated to 2 % of the households.\n\nA project was conducted and managed to provide a first description of the vulnerabilities that contribute to energy poverty risk in Malmö's multifamily and single-family housing stocks. In the single-family housing stock, the mapping of heating systems has provided an overview of how much oil, gas, and direct electric heating is being used, and where it is primarily being used. Combining this with household incomes shows where in Malmö households in high risk for energy poverty primarily reside which facilitates targeted measures to help alleviate their situation. In the multifamily housing stock, energy poverty diagnosis has been conducted through the use of survey data and 23 in-depth interviews on people's heating situation. The interviews gave insight into how tenants with warm rent still struggle to access sufficient warmth in their homes, and why access may be limited. In many cases, it had to do with old windows, old buildings, insufficient action by the landlord, bad or complicated relationship to the landlord (e.g. fear of eviction if complaining about cold), difficulties to reach or communicate with the landlord (e.g. language barriers), lack of knowledge on how to control/manage radiators, and lack of knowledge on how heating was billed, which led some people to decrease their heating due to fear of increased costs despite having warm rent. Regardless of the reason, it is common that people buy additional heating sources, such as heating fans or electric radiators, that lead to increased electricity bills that are then paid on top of the warm rent. In some of the vulnerable areas of Malmö, this is perceived as a financial burden that households still choose to pay in order to improve their well-being.

column17: According to the National Living Conditions and Income Survey (ICOR), in 2024, 15.7 per cent of people lived in households without the financial capacity to keep their homes adequately warmed (5.1 p.p. less than in 2023): https://www.ine.pt/xportal/xmain?xpid=INE&xpgid=ine_destaques&DESTAQUESdest_boui=736159693&DESTAQUESmodo=2. This value is greater than the European Union-27 countries on average (9.2%), however, Portugal is getting closer to the European average. \n\nFollowing the National Long-Term Strategy to Combat Energy Poverty 2023-2050 (https://files.diariodarepublica.pt/1s/2024/01/00500/0006900121.pdf) this indicator now comprises an important goal for the municipality to monitor and reduce. With this in mind, the Municipality of Porto carried out an Energy Poverty Study (https://porto.pobrezaenergetica.pt/resultados). Around 40 per cent of participants living in Porto admit to being uncomfortable with the temperature of their home in winter, while 23 per cent of respondents say they are equally uncomfortable with the temperature of their home in summer. However, the true extent of the problem may be greater. The most up-to-date value municipal value of 19.5% (1.3 percentage points below the national value) reported in 'Percentage of households or total population within the jurisdiction boundary that face energy poverty' is presented in the study 'Pobreza Energética em Portugal: Uma análise municipal' (https://www.novasbe.unl.pt/Portals/0/Files/Reports/2023/Nota_BS_Energy_dez_2023.pdf), which characterises energy poverty at local level by calculating the Municipal Energy Vulnerability Index (IVEM), using a statistical method that combines individual ICOR data with municipal data from the Census. The municipality's intention over the next few years is to increase information on this problem, as well as to define a local strategy to tackle energy poverty in the jurisdiction.

Only order of magnitude can be estimated here. Approximately 10% of the residents within Turku area living in detached houses (1% of all households) are at risk to suffer energy poverty. Similar statistics concerning apartment houses are not available, since e.g. heating (that covers the most of the households' energy consumption in Finland) is usually covered by the rent. Overall, 2% of the Finnish people suffer energy poverty.

The transition to renewable energy has lowered the prices of electricity and district heat in Turku. During COVID-19, Turku Energia was even able to offer an extra discount on the electricity courses. 

Then the energy crisis in winter 2022-2023 increased the risk of energy poverty. The City of Turku set a guiding example in electricity saving measures through its own actions. For example, the temperatures in the city's premises were lowered and the up-time of outdoor lighting was shortened. In addition, city residents were offered encouragement on electricity saving measures, lectures and instructions and tips. 

Energy poverty is a challenge that the energy crisis also focused on in Turku. The city cooperates closely with the energy company Turku Energia to develop clean and cost-effective energy production. This will help prevent energy poverty in Turku and the Turku region. Reasonably priced district heating is also a traction and retention factor.

column17:
De acordo com o Inquérito Nacional às Condições de Vida e Rendimentos (ICOR), em 2024, 15,7% das pessoas viviam em agregados familiares sem capacidade financeira para manter as suas casas adequadamente aquecidas (menos 5,1 p.p. do que em 2023): https://www.ine.pt/xportal/xmain?xpid=INE&xpgid=ine_destaques&DESTAQUESdest_boui=736159693&DESTAQUESmodo=2. Este valor é superior à média dos 27 países da União Europeia (9,2%), mas os resultados mostram que Portugal está a aproximar-se da média europeia.
A situação em termos de conforto térmico é ainda mais acentuada uma vez que, para além da proporção de agregados familiares que se encontravam nesta situação por motivos financeiros, acrescem 20.4% que vivem em alojamentos não suficientemente quentes no inverno por outros motivos, e que 29.9% vivem em alojamentos que não são adequadamente frescos no verão. 
Matosinhos desenvolveu, em 2024, o Plano de Ação para a Mitigação da Pobreza Energética (vertente incluída no Plano Municipal de Ação Climática) de forma a aumentar o grau de conhecimento sobre esta problemática no território, bem como definir um plano para a sua erradicação. Os dados nacionais (%) foram transpostos para a realidade local do Município de Matosinhos, permitindo identificar o valor de referência/ número de pessoas abrangidas por situação de pobreza energética. 
Além destes dados foi também considerado o Índice de Vulnerabilidade à Pobreza Energética (IPVE) - um índice desenvolvido pelo Centro de Investigação em Ambiente e Sustentabilidade da Universidade Nova de Lisboa (CENSE) e referenciado pela Estratégia Nacional de Longo Prazo de Combate à Pobreza Energética 2023 -2050 (ELPPE) como um trabalho de referência na temática. 
A avaliação deste índice no contexto municipal demonstra que o IPVE de aquecimento no Município de Matosinhos é de 7,30, o que coloca Matosinhos na posição 291 no ranking nacional (num total de 308 municípios). Este resultado revela que Matosinhos é um dos territórios com menor vulnerabilidade à pobreza energética na Área Metropolitana do Porto (que regista um resultado de 8,70) e um dos melhores classificados a nível nacional. 
À escala da freguesia, a União das Freguesias de Perafita, Lavra e Santa Cruz do Bispo é a que apresenta piores resultados (IPVE Aquecimento de 8,8) enquanto a União das Freguesia de São Mamede de Infesta e Senhora da Hora é a mais bem posicionada neste indicador (IPVE Aquecimento de 6.3).

column17: Não obstante os esforços já desenvolvidos, através de diversos projetos, no âmbito das cidades inteligentes, transição energética e descarbonização, o Município carece de um conhecimento claro, detalhado e holístico sobre a real dimensão da pobreza energética no seu território. Não obstante este facto, é possível através da análise de alguns indicadores indiretos inferir que é expectável que atualmente os níveis de pobreza energética no município de Évora sejam elevados. Em concreto, no ano de 2011, 758 alojamentos familiares em Évora não possuíam sistema de aquecimento e 3295 dependiam de uma lareira para aquecimento. No mesmo ano, 2544 munícipes beneficiaram do Rendimento Social de Inserção e 2085 alunos beneficiaram da Ação Social Escolar. Estando a pobreza energética associada às condições económicas da população, o número de beneficiários destas prestações sociais (indicadores de pobreza), também permite inferir a situação do município em relação a esta problemática. De forma a colmatar esta lacuna, em 2022 o município apresentou uma candidatura à \'Call for technical assistance to tackle energy poverty\', de forma a obter apoio técnico na elaboração do diagnóstico da atual situação municipal e indicação de soluções de combate efetivo à pobreza energética. Embora esta candidatura em concreto não tenha sido aprovada, o município, reconhecendo a importância desta problemática, pretende obter esta informação tão breve quanto possível, nomeadamente através da apresentação de candidaturas a iniciativas de natureza similar.

column17: A 2019 study conducted by Fisher, Sheehan, & Colton assessed the Home Energy Affordability Gap in states and counties across the country by household poverty level. In Kent County, households with incomes below 50% of the federal poverty level (FPL) spent about a third of their household income on home energy bills whereas households with incomes between 185-200% of the federal poverty level paid almost 7% of their household incomes on energy bills. At each FPL included in the study, households spent more than 6% of their household income on energy costs, which is considered energy burdened. While the analysis did not include data for households with incomes above 200% of the federal poverty level, generally the trend persists with higher income households spending less of their income on energy bills. Beyond household income level, localized data disaggregated by race/ethnicity is needed to capture the impact among community members.

Tampere and Finland do not have an official definition or threshold for energy poverty. In Finland, energy poverty has not been considered a significant societal issue that should be addressed separately from the social security system and other policy measures. The risk of energy poverty in Finland is mitigated by the energy efficiency of the building stock, a highly developed energy system, and one of the most advanced and comprehensive social security systems in the world.

Estimating the exact number of energy-poor households is challenging due to the complexity of the phenomenon and lack of comprehensive data. Ministry of the Environment (2015) states that there are 60,000-100,000 home-owning households at risk of energy poverty, but does not provide evidence or data on the actual quantitative number of energy-poor households in Finland. According to the most recent national assessment of energy poverty (2024), the risk groups in Finland include low-income residents living in detached houses, elderly people, and those living in energy-inefficient buildings.

Energy poverty has not received much attention historically because energy was relatively cheap and widely available. However, electricity and fuel prices have increased since autumn 2021 and are likely to remain higher than before. In 2022, Tampere conducted its first voluntary local review of the SDGs and identified energy poverty as a potential issue that may affect residents more in the future. However, mobility poverty was seen as a more central issue at the time.

LI - Low income
Households with a low income and assets below the asset threshold. For low incomes, the threshold value of 130 percent of the low-income threshold is used. The low-income threshold is a fixed amount that represents equal purchasing power for all years and all types of households. The threshold is derived from the social assistance level for a single person in 1979, when purchasing power was at its highest. For multi-person households, this threshold is adjusted to the size and composition of the household using equivalence factors. Because the low-income threshold is only indexed for price developments, this criterion is particularly suitable for comparisons over time. 
The asset threshold is the 90th percentile of the amount of assets excluding the home (i.e., the payment reserve) of all households within the Energy Poverty Monitor population for the 2019 reporting year. For the other years, the threshold value has been adjusted for inflation. 

LEK - Low energy quality
Households with low energy quality homes. Energy quality is a measure of how energy efficient a home is. The energy label is a well-known measure of energy quality. However, it has two major drawbacks: many homes do not have a label, and for those that do, the label is often out of date. A model has therefore been developed for the energy poverty monitor. The energy quality of a home is therefore a measure of how much energy a particular type of home consumes on average, under normal use and with a standard surface area. 
A home has low energy quality if the normalized expected energy bill is higher than the median normalized energy bill in 2019 (the threshold value). This threshold value is deliberately independent of the energy price or temperature, because this indicator concerns the long-term effects of a poor home on the energy bill.

In Norway, a high-income country with historically low electricity prices, energy poverty has barely been on the political agenda. However, many Norwegian households are increasingly at risk of living with energy poverty due to higher electricity prices, as experienced in the winters of 2021 and 2022. There is little research on this in the Norwegian context, but the few studies available indicate that it is an existing problem in Norway as well (source: https://www.globe.uio.no/english/include/research/projects/energy-poverty-in-norway/ and in Norwegian: https://www.fni.no/prosjekter/powerpoor).

What is being done in the area: 
The electricity support schemes, and now the new 'Norgespris', are responses to the rising energy prices, although there is a lot that could be done differently with this scheme, it can result in many households having lower expenses related to energy consumption.

A little more about the current support scheme: When the electricity price exceeds 0.73 NOK/kWh, the Norwegian state covers 90% of the difference up to 5,000 kWh/month.

A little more about 'Norgespris': 
From October 2025, households will be offered a fixed electricity price of 0.4 NOK/kWh excluding network rent. 

Other actions being done: 
Support schemes for energy efficiency through Enova and the housing bank, housing subsidies, national goals for energy efficiency, research and mapping through the power poor project mentioned above.

An article from 2021, estimating the amount of power poor inhabitants in Norway to be around 50 000 persons - at least 1% of Norway's population (source: https://www.nrk.no/norge/forsker_-50.000-opplever-energifattigdom-1.15729059)

Contexto y datos clave
•A nivel nacional, el 18,5 % de la población vive en situación de pobreza energética 
•En el departamento de Córdoba (donde se encuentra Montería), este porcentaje asciende al 63 % de la población 
•La pobreza energética en zonas rurales es 11 veces más alta que en zonas urbanas: 47,9 % rural vs 4,3 % urbano 
El umbral de pobreza energética puede ser:
•Económico: gastar más del 10 % de los ingresos en energía.
•Estimación de pobreza energética en Montería: Tomando datos poblacionales del DANE (aprox. 516 000 personas en total: 402 069 en zona urbana y 114 148 en rural)
• Población urbana: 402 069 × 4,3 % ≈ 17 287 personas en pobreza energética.
• Población rural: 114 148 × 47,9 % ≈ 54 693 personas en pobreza energética.
Total estimado: ≈ 71 980 personas de Montería estarían en situación de pobreza energética.
Conversión a viviendas: Suponiendo un promedio de ~4 personas por hogar:
71 980 / 4 ≈ 18 000 viviendas en pobreza energética.
Qué porcentaje representa del total municipal
Montería tiene aproximadamente 130 300 viviendas con servicio eléctrico (cobertura del 99,25 %)
Por tanto:
18 000 / 130 300 ≈ ~14 % de viviendas en pobreza energética.
Indicador	Valor estimado
Población urbana en pobreza energética	~17 287 personas
Población rural en pobreza energética	~54 693 personas
Total personas en pobreza energética	~71 980 personas
Viviendas afectadas (estimadas)	~18 000 viviendas
Porcentaje sobre viviendas totales	~14 %
consideraciones importantes
•El cálculo se basa en promedios departamentales por zonas urbanos/rurales, no en datos de Montería desagregados.
•Las estimaciones consideran acceso y calidad de energía, combustibles para cocinar, iluminación, refrigeración y confort térmico (dimensiones del Índice de Pobreza Energética Multidimensional - IMPE) 
•No se incluyen variables como pobreza monetaria o multidimensional general: se centra exclusivamente en penurias relacionadas con servicios energéticos.
•Para obtener cifras exactas, sería necesario un estudio local especializado o cifras municipales disponibles por barrios o estratos socioeconómicos.
Conclusión: Se estima que en Montería, aproximadamente el 14 % de las viviendas (~18 000 hogares) enfrentan pobreza energética, lo que corresponde a unas 72 000 personas, con brechas marcadas entre zonas rurales y urbanas.

Registered or actual residents of New Taipei City whose average total household income does not exceed NT$16,000 per person per month, and whose total family-owned real estate assets do not exceed NT$4.2 million.

Definition of Lower-Middle-Income Households:
Registered or actual residents of New Taipei City whose average total household income does not exceed NT$24,000 per person per month (the minimum cost of living), and whose total family-owned real estate assets do not exceed NT$6.3 million.

Low number of households spending over 10 % of income on energy
The qualitative study defines energy poverty as households spending more than 10 % of their income on heating. While a few low-income respondents in the study did meet this threshold, the majority did not.

The study focuses on owner-occupied households with low income. Even within this group, several interviewees had significant home equity or savings, supporting renovation investments or reliably covering energy expenses.

In our municipality, such financial resilience is more widespread, given strong local property values and prudent household planning, further reducing risk.

There is a lack of detailed data regarding energy poverty in the Beşiktaş district. To properly assess energy poverty, essential data such as the number of households and areas without access to energy are needed, but this information has not been obtained. However, data on the number of households receiving coal assistance within Beşiktaş have been provided, which can be used as an indicator to assess energy poverty.

The households receiving coal aid in Beşiktaş indicate that fossil fuel use still persists and that these households may be at risk of experiencing energy poverty. In neighborhoods such as Ortaköy, Abbasağa, and Vişnezade, a small number of households receive coal aid, and the use of traditional stoves suggests these households may face difficulties accessing modern energy systems.

While fossil fuel use is decreasing overall in Beşiktaş, improving access to renewable energy remains crucial. It has been emphasized that to combat energy poverty, it is important to eliminate fossil fuel use entirely and accelerate the transition to renewable energy sources. Beşiktaş Municipality has several projects aimed at promoting sustainable energy solutions in this regard.

In conclusion, households receiving coal assistance in Beşiktaş can be considered as potentially experiencing energy poverty. However, a more comprehensive analysis is required to fully evaluate the overall energy poverty situation in the district. Issues related to access to energy and economic inequalities have not been fully identified.

No specific threshold or official criterion has been used to define and measure energy poverty in Beşiktaş. Therefore, the available data on households facing energy poverty is limited, and a more thorough investigation is necessary.

Ele contempla três eixos: (i) o acesso físico a fontes de energia, medido, por exemplo, pela existência de conexão ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), (ii) a posse de equipamentos, como televisão, geladeira, refrigerador e acesso à internet e (iii) e a acessibilidade, ou capacidade de pagamento pelo uso da energia, medido pelo peso das despesas com energia na despesa total da residência. No artigo, o Multidimensional energy poverty index (MEPI) foi calculado por estado, diferenciando a população urbana e rural. No AdaptaBrasil MCTI, com o intuito de se chegar a um valor único para cada estado, o indicador foi ponderado pela população urbana e rural.
O indicador MEPI foi obtido no artigo referenciado anteriormente e a população rural e urbana foi obtida na Pesquisa de Orçamentos Familiares (POF) 2017-2018, do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE).

In 2018, the Town of Bridgewater sent a community-wide survey on energy poverty to every household in Town. In total, 585 responses to the survey were received, corresponding to a return rate of around 15% of households. The survey demonstrated an energy poverty rate of 38.5% based on the definition of energy poverty described above. The number of households living in Bridgewater at the time was extrapolated from population projections based on 2016 Census data.

In 2022, researchers from McGill University conducted a detailed household survey to verify and refine our understanding of energy poverty in the community. Again, over 500 households were surveyed, and the energy poverty rate of 38% was confirmed through this approach. The energy poverty threshold used for the survey was 2 x the median national spending on energy, or 5.4% of gross household income.

In 2025, researchers from McGill University conducted a second detailed household survey to follow up on the status of energy poverty in the community. Again, over 500 households were surveyed, and the energy poverty rate of 33% was confirmed through this approach. The energy poverty threshold used for the survey was 2 x the median national spending on energy, or 5.4% of gross household income.

Afecta la salud pública, por el uso de combustibles sólidos.

Indikator Utama Energy Poverty

Rasio Elektrifikasi (RE)

Persentase rumah tangga yang sudah memiliki akses listrik (diukur dari pelanggan PLN/non-PLN).

Kota Manado sudah mencapai >99%, sehingga gap akses listrik hampir tertutup.

Rasio Desa Berlistrik (RDB)

Persentase desa/kelurahan yang sudah terhubung listrik.

Di Manado, seluruh kelurahan sudah berlistrik.

Konsumsi Energi Per Kapita

Total kWh listrik rata-rata yang digunakan per orang/tahun.

Indikator ini penting untuk membedakan antara akses (sekadar tersambung listrik) dan kecukupan energi untuk memenuhi kebutuhan dasar.

Proporsi Pengeluaran Rumah Tangga untuk Energi

Persentase pengeluaran listrik, LPG, dan BBM dalam total pengeluaran rumah tangga.

Jika >10% dari total pengeluaran, dikategorikan sebagai energy burdened household.

Jenis Bahan Bakar yang Digunakan untuk Memasak

Indikator transisi energi: berapa banyak rumah tangga masih menggunakan kayu bakar/arang vs LPG/listrik.

Semakin banyak rumah tangga memakai bahan bakar modern (LPG, listrik), semakin rendah energy poverty.

Jam Layanan Listrik per Hari (Reliability of Supply)

Mengukur keandalan pasokan: frekuensi pemadaman, jam layanan harian.

Meskipun RE tinggi, kualitas pasokan bisa memengaruhi energy poverty.

De acordo com o Inquérito Nacional às Condições de Vida e Rendimentos (ICOR), em 2024, 15,7% das pessoas viviam em agregados familiares sem capacidade financeira para manter as suas casas adequadamente aquecidas (menos 5,1 p.p. do que em 2023): https://www.ine.pt/xportal/xmain?xpid=INE&xpgid=ine_destaques&DESTAQUESdest_boui=736159693&DESTAQUESmodo=2. Este valor é superior à média dos 27 países da União Europeia (9,2%), mas os resultados mostram que Portugal está a aproximar-se da média europeia.
A situação em termos de conforto térmico é ainda mais acentuada uma vez que, para além da proporção de agregados familiares que se encontravam nesta situação por motivos financeiros, acrescem 20.4% que vivem em alojamentos não suficientemente quentes no inverno por outros motivos, e que 29.9% vivem em alojamentos que não são adequadamente frescos no verão. 
Segundo a Estratégia Nacional de Combate à Pobreza Energética, em 2021, 16,6% da população a viver em agregados não tinha capacidade para manter a casa adequadamente aquecida, uma diminuição relativamente a 2020, cujo indicador era de 17,5%.
O valor municipal de 19.5% referente a 2021 reportado em “Percentage of households or total population within the jurisdiction boundary that face energy poverty^” está presente no estudo de 2023 “Pobreza Energética em Portugal: Uma análise municipal” (https://www.novasbe.unl.pt/Portals/0/Files/Reports/2023/Nota_BS_Energy_dez_2023.pdf) que caracteriza a pobreza energética ao nível local calculando o Índice de Vulnerabilidade Energética Municipal (IVEM), através de um método estatístico que combina os dados individuais do ICOR com os dados municipais dos Censos de 2021.
Ainda dentro deste âmbito, a Maia integrou em setembro de 2024 a Rede EmPowerIngUs que permitirá, no futuro, ter acesso a valores de indicadores de pobreza energética que traduzirão, de uma forma mais aproximada, a realidade local.

Penetapan kategori kemiskinan energi (energy poverty) bagi rumah tangga di Kabupaten Sumbawa dapat didasarkan pada kemampuan rumah tangga dalam memenuhi kebutuhan energi minimum, khususnya listrik. Pada pendekatan berbasis biaya listrik (expenditure-based energy poverty), rumah tangga dikategorikan miskin energi apabila proporsi pengeluaran listriknya berada di atas atau melampaui batas kewajaran dibandingkan pendapatannya, sehingga menimbulkan beban ekonomi berlebihan.

1. Penggunaan Prinsip “High Energy Expenditure Burden”

Rumah tangga dapat diklasifikasikan sebagai miskin energi apabila:

Persentase pengeluaran listrik ≥10% dari total pengeluaran rumah tangga per bulan.
Ambang ini lazim digunakan dalam kajian nasional dan internasional untuk menentukan beban energi yang tidak proporsional.

Pada rumah tangga berpenghasilan rendah, batas ini dapat turun menjadi 6-8%, karena sensitivitas pengeluaran lebih tinggi.

2. Perbandingan dengan Penghasilan Minimum Regional

Di Kabupaten Sumbawa, penetapan miskin energi juga dapat merujuk pada indikator ekonomi lokal:

Upah Minimum Kabupaten (UMK) dan garis kemiskinan BPS dijadikan dasar untuk menilai apakah rumah tangga tersebut mampu membiayai kebutuhan listrik dasar tanpa mengorbankan kebutuhan esensial lain.

Rumah tangga yang membayar listrik melebihi kemampuan daya beli minimal dapat dikategorikan sebagai energy stressed households.

3. Pola Konsumsi Listrik yang Tidak Mencapai Kebutuhan Minimum

Sebuah rumah tangga juga dapat dianggap miskin energi apabila:

Daya listrik sangat rendah (misal 450 VA subsidi) tetapi masih tidak mampu membayar tagihan.

Konsumsi listrik per bulan sangat kecil (misal <40 kWh/bulan), mencerminkan penghematan terpaksa akibat keterbatasan ekonomi, bukan karena efisiensi.

4. Indikator Tambahan yang Dapat Digunakan Pemerintah Daerah

Untuk konteks Kabupaten Sumbawa, penetapan miskin energi berbasis listrik dapat diperkuat dengan indikator lokal, antara lain:

Tunggakan pembayaran listrik rutin yang berulang.

Ketidakmampuan meningkatkan daya listrik meskipun kebutuhan meningkat (misalnya untuk keperluan usaha kecil, alat pendingin, penerangan memadai).

Ketergantungan pada sumber penerangan alternatif seperti genset kecil, pelita, atau solar cell murah yang tidak mencukupi kebutuhan.

Rumah tangga berada pada desa kategori tertinggal atau sangat tertinggal (berdasarkan IDM), yang biasanya memiliki biaya energi tidak proporsional.

5. Kaitan dengan Kondisi Sumbawa

Kabupaten Sumbawa memiliki tingkat kemiskinan sekitar ±11-12%, serta akses listrik PLN sekitar ±92%. Namun, kemiskinan energi masih dapat terjadi karena:

Tarikan tagihan listrik yang tinggi bagi rumah tangga berpenghasilan rendah, terutama ketika pemakaian meningkat.

Keterbatasan kemampuan membayar listrik prabayar.

Ketergantungan pada daya kecil (450-900 VA) yang membatasi kenyamanan hidup dan produktivitas.

Additionally, the report highlights related challenges:
- 4.7% of households have experienced disconnection from the electricity grid due to late or non-payment of electricity bills, indicating financial strain related to energy costs.
- 11.9% of households reported difficulties in paying electricity bills, often due to low income, high electricity prices, or challenges in accessing payment systems (e.g., lack of familiarity with digital payment methods or logistical issues for elderly households).
These figures suggest that while access to the electricity grid is universal (100%), a notable portion of households in Hue City face energy poverty due to the high proportion of income spent on energy.

column17:
O limite de até 10% da renda gasta em serviços energéticos é amplamente reconhecido como o critério mais consistente e internacionalmente aceito para definir pobreza energética. Esse indicador surgiu originalmente nas políticas do Reino Unido na década de 1980, quando se observou que famílias que precisavam gastar mais de 10% de sua renda disponível em energia — seja para eletricidade, gás, aquecimento ou cocção — estavam em situação de privação energética, pois comprometiam recursos essenciais para alimentação, moradia e saúde. Desde então, o parâmetro foi adotado ou adaptado em diversos estudos e iniciativas internacionais, incluindo o World Bank, a International Energy Agency (IEA), a Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS) e programas regionais da América Latina e União Europeia voltados à transição energética justa e à erradicação da pobreza multidimensional.

O critério dos 10% equilibra duas dimensões principais da pobreza energética: acessibilidade econômica e uso adequado da energia. Ele não se limita à existência de infraestrutura elétrica, mas avalia se a família tem condições reais de utilizar energia suficiente e segura para atender às suas necessidades básicas — cozinhar, iluminar, refrigerar alimentos e manter conforto térmico. No contexto brasileiro, essa medida dialoga com a Tarifa Social de Energia Elétrica (TSEE), que garante descontos progressivos para famílias de baixa renda, exatamente para evitar que o gasto com energia ultrapasse uma fração desproporcional do orçamento doméstico.

No caso de Vitória de Santo Antão (PE), o uso desse limite é adequado porque o município apresenta:
	1.	Acesso praticamente universal à eletricidade (Censo 2022 - IBGE), porém com elevada proporção de domicílios em vulnerabilidade de renda.
	2.	Uma parcela significativa da população cadastrada na Tarifa Social, que tem como base o mesmo princípio de garantir que os custos energéticos não ultrapassem a capacidade de pagamento das famílias.
	3.	Condições climáticas quentes e úmidas, que elevam o uso de refrigeração e ventilação, aumentando o consumo energético doméstico e, consequentemente, o impacto na renda das famílias de menor poder aquisitivo.

Além de sua ampla aceitação, o limite de 10% possui base empírica sólida. Estudos da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) e da Energy Poverty Observatory (EPOV) da União Europeia demonstram que esse valor é suficientemente sensível para identificar populações em vulnerabilidade sem superestimar a incidência do problema. Famílias que gastam mais de 10% de sua renda com energia tendem a apresentar privação térmica, endividamento e insegurança alimentar, por terem de reduzir gastos com outros bens essenciais.

Em termos de padronização, o uso do limite de 10% permite que os resultados de Vitória de Santo Antão sejam comparáveis com os de outras cidades brasileiras e internacionais que reportam ao CDP-ICLEI Track e aos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS 7 - Energia Acessível e Limpa). Essa escolha também facilita o alinhamento com programas federais e estaduais que utilizam critérios semelhantes de vulnerabilidade socioenergética.

Portanto, o município adota o limite de até 10% da renda familiar comprometida com serviços energéticos (eletricidade, gás de cozinha e outras fontes modernas) para classificar a pobreza energética. Esse parâmetro expressa o ponto em que os custos energéticos passam a representar uma sobrecarga desproporcional sobre o orçamento das famílias, comprometendo o bem-estar e a resiliência socioeconômica local.

Fontes e referências:
	1.	Censo Demográfico 2022 - IBGE - Acesso a energia e combustíveis para cozinhar:
https://sidra.ibge.gov.br/tabela/8127
	2.	Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) - Energy Access and Affordability Framework:
https://www.iea.org/topics/energy-access
	3.	Banco Mundial - Understanding Energy Poverty:
https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/energy/brief/understanding-energy-poverty
	4.	Energy Poverty Observatory (EPOV) - European Commission:
https://energy-poverty.ec.europa.eu/observatory-overview/methodology_en
	5.	Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) - Tarifa Social de Energia Elétrica:
https://www.gov.br/pt-br/servicos/solicitar-tarifa-social-de-energia-eletrica
	6.	Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável - ODS 7 (Energia Acessível e Limpa):
https://brasil.un.org/pt-br/sdgs/7

Em síntese, esse limite de 10% é o ponto de referência internacional e nacionalmente reconhecido para definir pobreza energética, sendo o mais apropriado para o contexto socioeconômico de Vitória de Santo Antão e para o reporte ao CDP.

The energy profile of the City of Balanga, as drawn from PENELCO data and the Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA), shows a city that has already achieved near-universal electrification across all barangays. In 2018, the city's total electricity consumption was estimated at 577,316 MWh, with the residential sector accounting for the majority share at 50.82%, or about 293,409 MWh. This underscores the importance of household demand in shaping the city's energy use pattern. The low-voltage sector, which includes commercial establishments, public buildings, street lighting, irrigation, and small industries, contributed 24.59% or roughly 142,012 MWh, while the high-voltage industrial sector accounted for 14.59% or about 84,226 MWh of total consumption. The remaining share came from other special categories under PENELCO's franchise.

Balanga's electricity supply is drawn from the national grid through PENELCO, with significant sourcing from large independent power producers such as SMC Global Power and GNPower. Much of this supply mix still relies on coal-fired generation, which directly links electricity consumption to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. For 2018, Balanga's electricity consumption contributed approximately 5,043 tCO₂e, which represents around 2.8% of the city's total GHG emissions of 182,941.4 tCO₂e.

While electricity use accounts for a relatively small fraction of Balanga's overall emissions compared with dominant sectors such as transport and solid waste, its impact is not insignificant. The data highlights two critical points: first, that households are the largest single energy-consuming group, and second, that the carbon intensity of the current energy supply presents both a challenge and an opportunity. By advancing energy efficiency initiatives, encouraging the adoption of rooftop solar and other renewables, and promoting sustainable practices across residential, commercial, and industrial sectors, Balanga can gradually decouple its electricity demand from coal dependence. In doing so, the city not only reduces its GHG footprint but also enhances energy affordability and security for its residents.

El municipio de Envigado no ha hecho un estudio de pobreza energética, pero en la encuesta de calidad de vida que se realiza anualmente se miden los porcentaje de acceso a la energía (cobertura servicio de electricidad del 100%). En Colombia, aunque se han desarrollado varios estudios, todavía no se ha realizado una metodología y,
por ende, un cálculo de la pobreza energética a nivel nacional y regional, lo que ha llevado a que las políticas
públicas y la asignación de recursos no esté enfocada o priorizada en las regiones que más lo necesitan y
que permiten maximizar la contribución del sector energético al desarrollo sostenible del país.
De acuerdo con un estudio del orden nacional, los elementos que se tienen en cuenta para medir la pobreza energética son: 
Iluminación: Cobertura del 100% para zona urbana y rural
Confort térmico: Cobertura del 27,03% en zona urbana y del 64,7% en zona rural
Cocción: Cobertura del 100% en zona urbana con energía eléctrica y gas domiciliario y del 24,25% con energía contaminante en zona rural
Tecnologías de la Información y la Comunicación: Cobertura del 100% en zona urbana y del 60% en zona rural
Equidad energética del 65,62% en zona urbana y del 53,16% en zona rural
